speechtext: In view of the fact that the new Indian Act has been introduced and we shall be discussing it shortly, I do not propose to make any general remarks at this point. However, I think it might expedite the consideration of these items having to do with Indian affairs if the minister would give us a review of what has been accomplished in the improvement of welfare conditions on the reserves during the last year, what is proposed for the coming year, what has been done to increase school accommodation, and what other improvements are being made.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
subsubtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
If the hon. member will permit I should like to make a short statement with respect to education and welfare, and perhaps we can leave any other subjects until the Indian Act amendment bill is up for second reading, or answer specific questions on the relevant items in the estimates.
Shortly before the Easter recess I tabled an annual report under section 113 of the Indian Act which showed that, during the fiscal year 1949-50, 310 Indians had been enfranchised. During the same period around 6,000 Indian babies were born. This indicates that the number of Indians accepting enfranchisement is much lower than the natural increase in Indian population, and this must be borne in mind in welfare planning and education.
In such planning the recommendations of the joint parliamentary committee on the
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Indian Act are of great value to the department. As many members know, this committee sat in 1946, 1947, and 1948, during which time it held 129 meetings. In addition, the committee visited most Indian reserves, in eastern Canada. The bill which I had the honour to present on Wednesday, June 7, is in many details the result of the good work of that committee.
Two government activities that are of primary importance to the welfare of Indians are those relating to health and education. Health now comes under the Department of National Health and Welfare, and the substantial increase in the amount now voted for Indian health services compared to that voted ten years ago is an indication of the importance attached to the problem by the government and parliament.
So far as education is concerned, I am glad to report substantial improvement. During the past four years, roughly the post-war period, total enrolment in Indian schools has risen from 19,622 to 23,409. Attendance has improved from a percentage of 79-91 to 88-23. In addition to those attending Indian schools, 1,180 Indian children were registered in provincial schools in elementary grades, and 465 in secondary grades, an over-all total of 25,054 Indian pupils in educational classes. Those attending school in grades above grade 8 number 834. To bring educational facilities to as many children as possible, the government approved a school-building program extending over a period of five years. This year, 1950, will be the third year of this construction plan. The number of schools erected can be illustrated by the fact that the government employed 285 day school teachers in 1946, and is now employing 450. The provision of over 100 new schoolrooms is planned for this year. When it is realized that each new schoolroom has to be equipped, staffed, and maintained, it will be appreciated that the cost of operation must increase, and that this year's estimates have been kept down.
In spite of an increasing teacher shortage, the standard of the teaching staff has been improved. The number of non-qualified teachers has been reduced in two years to one-fifth of the staff instead of one-third, and this change is continuing. During the same period the percentage of teachers with first-class certificates has risen from 27 to 40. Day school attendance has improved steadily as a result of family allowances, the higher calibre of the teachers employed, improvement of classroom techniques and equipment, and the awakening interest of Indian parents. In accordance with recommendations of the joint parliamentary committee, the department has
3710	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration been directing its efforts to having more Indian children admitted to provincial schools.
It is the policy of the department to alleviate hardship of those unable to provide for themselves, and to encourage Indians to be self-sufficient through the provision of occupational assistance. Approximately 2,000 Indian houses were repaired, and approximately 1,300 new houses erected during 1949-50, the extent of assistance in each case depending on the ability of the Indian to share in construction. Provision is made in the estimates for similar work in 1950-51, the number of new houses and other works and structures totalling 894.
Assistance is provided for Indian fishermen and farmers by the acquisition of stock, equipment and seed; for the blind; for the rehabilitation of tubercular Indians and their dependents following discharge from hospital, and for the indigent.
During the past fiscal year, provision was made for the employment of nine social workers. This is something of a new venture. It is the function of these workers to conduct surveys on reserves with reference to social conditions, particularly in matters of delinquency, destitution and the care of the aged. They will encourage the formation of homemakers clubs, and will assist in the establishment of young people leaving schools. An important phase of their duties will be liaison with municipal and provincial welfare agencies and local offices of the Canadian National Institute for the Blind.
In keeping with government policy of careful attention to the developing needs of the Indian population, I am pleased to inform the house that, effective July 1 of this year, the special allowance payable to aged Indians seventy years of age and over will be increased from $8 to $25 per month.
The present $8 monthly cash payment is supplemental to regular relief, and is intended to enable the aged to purchase extras. The additional cash allowance will, of course, supersede present relief issues. The increased payment represents a new departure in that many aged Indians will be entrusted with the management of these funds, and be responsible for their own needs. This development is therefore a significant step toward granting the Indian a greater measure of responsibility for the direction of his own affairs. To judge the amount of this payment in true perspective it is necessary to bear in mind that aged Indians enjoy certain special privileges, amongst which I would list complete medical care and residence on tax-free land.

I am very glad, as I am sure other hon. members are, to hear this statement. I am particularly pleased to hear that the old age allowance for Indians is to be increased to $25 per month. The fact that those aged Indians have not enjoyed the right to the old age pension in common with other aged Canadians, has in the past been an anomaly. It certainly is good news that the situation has been corrected. The increase in the number of Indian children attending school is also satisfactory. I am glad to hear that the building program is going along so well.
I should like to ask the minister how many children are attending each of the grades from seven to twelve inclusive. One of the great deficiencies of Indian education in the past has been the fact that few Indians have gone into the higher grades. The result has been few of them have received the training which would enable them to secure jobs in competition with white people. I trust that situation is gradually being overcome. It is bound to be a slow process, but I believe that with the improvement in educational facilities that has taken place, and the further improvements which I understand are in prospect, there should be an increase in the number of Indian children attending the higher grades. This would equip them to compete with the white population for employment, and thus enable them to improve their standard of living.
The minister said that 310 Indians were enfranchised. Will he tell us whether those Indians were enfranchised voluntarily? In other words, did they ask for enfranchisement or were they enfranchised against their will? Were they just thrown out of the reserve and told they were citizens and had to look after themselves? Perhaps there are some in each class; can the minister tell us how many were voluntarily enfranchised and how many were involuntarily enfranchised?

speechtext:
I am delighted to hear from the minister that the Indians are going to get this $25 a month of their old age pension. It is the best news I have heard for a long time with regard to Indians. I have not had an opportunity to study it. I did not know that it was coming. I do not know whether there will be a means test attached to it or not, but I hope for the best. I am sure that the rest of the members who were on the Indian affairs committee and sat for three years will be pleased to see the results of their labours. Every member of the committee did his utmost to bring to the attention of the government-and that included those on the government side as well-the hardships suffered by and the treatment accorded to the Indians in the past. I am going to reserve what I have to say until the Indian Act is being considered, in order that I shall not be covering the same subjects twice, but there are one or two questions I want to ask in passing; they pertain to the administration of the department.
Has the minister given any further consideration to the setting up of a claims commission? Every Indian who comes to your office or to mine digs back into the past and produces some agreement that he obtained from the King of France, or perhaps the King of England or Queen Victoria; and he tells you that it has never been fulfilled. It is necessary that we clear up the thinking of the Indian. If he still teaches his grandson that we owe him something, then we should straighten that matter up. The only way that can be done is by a claims commission which will look into these matters. I am not going to refer to any province other than Manitoba, although I have travelled over the reserves in nine different provinces. The Indians immediately lay on my desk the agreement they got in 1871, or something else, and claim that it has not been fulfilled. I do not know how the minister can fulfil it unless he sets up a claims commission. We have a new minister and perhaps he has not had the opportunity of looking into it. I hope that he will see whether it is possible or feasible to do that sort of thing, sb that we may let the Indians know where they really stand.
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
I had some Indians here this week to see me; they produced some documents that were supposed to be written in 1792. We have to get this thing straightened up. When it is, I know that the Canadian government will get credit for the way in which they have handled the Indians instead of the criticism there has been for a great many years.
I wonder if the minister can tell me whether any more houses have been built at Norway House-that is, houses for the old people. Some were built when I represented that part of the country, and they were a success so far as I could see when I visited them. Has the administration carried out its intention to build more houses at Cross lake and in other places in the north? Will the minister indicate also what the situation is with regard to the Indians in Newfoundland, because evidently they are not on reserves there as they are in other parts of Canada. Has the department taken further steps to see to it that the Indian agent is living nearer the reserve than he has been living in the past? I drew the attention of the minister's predecessor to the fact that sometimes the Indian agent was living 200 miles from the reserve. Has that situation been corrected? I think my other questions can wait until later.

I think I have cashed far more of these relief cheques than any other member who has ever been in the House of Commons. The Indian has always been given a slip which listed the quantities of goods that he would be supplied with. The price was not designated. The store was usually the one which was closest to the Indian village. Therefore we received the business from the Indians on their own volition.
I have always found the Indian agents very efficient. If they found that an Indian was being charged too much for a 49-pound sack of flour, the Indian agent himself was the first one to step in, in the interest of the government, and say to the Indian: "Probably it would be advisable for you to take that slip to a store that does not overcharge"-not the Indian, but the Indian department; because after all it was always the quantity of goods that was given to him, not a specific amount for the goods.

Mr. Chairman, I was pleased when this government saw fit to set up the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, and even more pleased when they appointed the hon. member for Grey-Bruce as its minister. I wish to express not only my own congratulations but the good wishes of the electors of my constituency as well. .The hon. minister is my neighbour and colleague, and I know that all problems confronting this department will be dealt with seriously and fairly.
The constituency which I represent is largely rural, with many progressive towns and villages, and they are truly happy people. Our farmers are second to none in Canada, or for that matter in the world; they are breeders of choice livestock as well as producers of excellent agricultural products.
Our towns and villages keep abreast of the times in modern manufacturing, and are producing commercial goods which find ready markets throughout the world. Labour relations are of the standard where employees and employers settle their differences, if any, in an amicable way.
In the constituency of Bruce we have two Indian reserves. These Indians are progressive. A large number are expanding in modern farming; many are employed in the industrial factories of our towns, and of course many more are engaged in fishing and trapping. I am pleased that this department is taking steps to improve the position of the Indian in the welfare of the country. We must not forget these people blazed many of the early trails in this country. The same sun shines on them, the same rain rains on them, as on the rest of us. Why should not the same rights be given them? When the call came for them to don the uniform in defence of our country, they did so in no small numbers, and I shall be glad to support any move that would raise their status.
May I add that I was pleased with the announcement the minister made this morning. I am sure it will improve the living conditions and educational opportunities of Indians throughout the country.

The constituency of Bruce extends for 140 miles as a peninsula with a coast line of over 200 miles. Lake Huron borders its shores on the west and the Georgian bay on the eastern side of the peninsula.

I should like to have the minister explain the method that is used by his department in renting premises. The law of the country seems to be clear with regard to most transactions by departments of government, but I am afraid it is not quite as good as it should be as to the renting of premises. We find certain general provisions laid down for all departments, including the Department of Public Works, I assume, in the Public Works Act, section 36. This section reads as follows:
Whenever any works are to be executed under the direction of any department of the government, the minister having charge of such department shall invite tenders by public advertisement for the execution of such works, except in cases
(a)	of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest; or
[Mr. Fournier (Hull).)
(b)	in which from the nature of the work it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department; or
(c)	where the estimated cost of the work is less than $5,000 and it appears to the minister, in view of the nature of the work, that it is not advisable to invite tenders.
Then there is this further provision in subsection 2 of the same section:
Whenever in case of any work tenders are required to be or are invited, the minister having charge of the department concerned shall submit all tenders received therefor to the governor in council-
That is, of course, to the cabinet.
-and the contract for the work shall be awarded under the direction of the governor in council.
I had something to say to the minister in the session last fall, and early in the present session, with regard to the government constructing buildings. I was referring to the Alvin building in Vancouver. I am not going into that matter any further today, but Mr. Chairman will recall there was a good deal of dispute about the way that work was handled. Today I want to go on to the question of the government renting buildings.
I find this provision in section 39 which reads:
Notwithstanding anything in this act, or in any other act contained, any public work not required for public purposes may be sold or leased, under the authority of the governor in council;-
The cabinet must approve the leasing by the government to someone else of one of these properties. The section continues:
. . . and the proceeds of such sale or lease shall be accounted for- as public moneys; Provided that such public works shall be so sold or leased by tender or at auction after public advertisement, unless it is otherwise authorized by the governor in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext: What are those last words?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext:
". . . unless it is otherwise
authorized by the governor in council." In other words where the government has a building with which it is finished, and the decision is made to sell or lease that building, either tenders must be called or the building must be sold at auction after public advertisement.
We find this position in Vancouver. The Department of Public Works, acting for the government, has rented certain buildings as postal stations. Earlier in the session I received a return showing these different stations. There are about eight which could be called postal stations, and they are small stations scattered about the city, and separate of course from the main Vancouver post office. Five of those postal stations have been rented from firms which, it cannot be disputed, are firms owned or controlled by friends of the government, by active leading Liberals. In

some way these people are able to find out when there is to be a postal station rented. It is obvious that they have what might be described as the inside track. When there is to be renting to the government, it is comparatively easy to finance the construction of a building. The rentals are always ample. In these cases I believe it would be found that the rentals, to say the least, are not too small. In these deals there is not the proper protection for the public.
I cannot find anything in the statutes which provides that when the government is going to rent premises it shall call for tenders or go through some other procedure which would ensure that everyone had a fair chance. Perhaps more important, it would mean that the price of the rental to the government would be lower. There can be no question about what has happened in these cases. I have the street addresses here, and the amounts paid to the firms from which the buildings are leased. These men may have the land, or they go out and buy the land, and then put up a building. They secure a good lease from the government. That sort of thing should be stopped. It is not in accordance with the provisions I have read from the Public Works Act. It brings the whole business of the Canadian government into disrepute with the people who know of such deals, and it does not take long for news to get around the city that that sort of thing is going on. The real estate people all know it; the contractors soon get to know it, and the effect is bad. I am quite sure that the minister himself would admit that it is bad business from the point of view of the country. If under the present legislation he is unable to stop that sort of thing, he should ask for an amendment to the act. The Canadian people are entitled to some better method of doing business.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra is right with regard to section 36, as to asking for tenders for works not undertaken by my department, and the three exceptions he mentioned: an emergency or an urgent case; if the work can be done more properly by the officials of the crown, and particularly when the cost is under $5,000. In this last year and after all the questions that were put in this chamber, I have been looking into this act thoroughly to see if we have often derogated from that section. I can tell my hon. friend that there are very few cases that my officials could not justify under this section when they made the recommendation that I sign to council. I will not say that everything in that department is perfect, but I must rely to a great extent on the advice of my officials. If they make
Supply-Public Works
mistakes and I sign, then I have to give the explanation and I am responsible to parliament. I know that.
I do not know whether we could make a change in section 36. It is quite general. The principle is that, having prepared the plans and specifications, we call for tenders. I sign these calls for tenders every week, and all through the country. I think it is in the exceptional case-and I could give a few cases around here-that tenders were not called because my officials and my advisers told me that nobody would try to give a firm price on the work to be undertaken. As an example, I mention the east block. When we started off with the east block, we saw the old building but we did not know what was in the building.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext: That is a repair job.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext:
Yes. But when we get through with it, it will be a new building. That is one of the jobs where we keep only the shell, I should say. No contractor would undertake a job like that on a firm price; and we did not call for tenders but came to an agreement on a fixed fee, a method which has the least objectionable features of any when getting other than a firm price. When it went over a certain amount the percentage was so small that I do not think anybody would criticize.
As to the second point, with regard to renting space, we do not rent space for ourselves except in a few cases-and I am speaking of the Department of Public Works -but every day there come into the office from all over the country requests from the other nineteen or twenty departments of government asking for space in this place and that. The first question we put to them is this: In what location do you need space? They will give us the kind of block in which they should have this post office, let us say. That is the first step that we take. When we have that information, our field men or resident architect in the town or district will send out people to make a survey of the properties. I have been thinking of the method of asking for tenders for renting space, but I cannot see how it would operate. When they say they need in that ward or in that part of Vancouver a postal station, even if we indicate the exact location of the post office or the postal station, there would be only one or two parties who could say: We will rent it to you at such a price. If I say: I want No. 50 Main street in my town for a postal station, I go to the owner of No. 50 Main street. I need not call for tenders, but I will try to negotiate with him to see at what price he will rent space.

Supply-Public Works
I cannot see the tender feature in renting space. What we do is this. We have here in Ottawa a branch of my department headed by Mr. Boucher, who has been in the service for years. He is the head of the leases branch of the department, and with his other officials has quite a wide experience. When we meet difficult cases and the cases cannot be settle ^ in the district, Mr. Boucher or one of his associates goes out to investigate. But we arrive at renting space by negotiation with the party. We have the current price and the unit price of space in that district and we base our offer on those prices. A mistake may be made in the price that we pay. It can happen every day. In transactions with regard to property or renting space, there is no definite figure that two people will agree on. In the first years I was in the department my experience was astounding. We would ask for tenders for a building which we estimated would cost $200,000. We would receive estimates that would go up to half a million dollars, and others which were $50,000 less. There is no absolute or definite figure.
The responsibility I have in this regarct is quite onerous. Nearly every day I have got to use my own judgment, to see whether, on all the information I receive from my officials, we are right or wrong. I cannot say definitely whether the cost will be $1.98 per square foot or $2.05; but I take all the material they bring before me and I say: What is this company paying? What are the provincial governments paying? We get an average as to the price. When I am requested to get space at such and such a number on such and such a street in such and such a city, if the hon. member could devise a system by which I should ask for tenders, I would not object to trying even to change the act; but I would not know how to make it operate. That is the advice my officials give me.
The other point the hon. gentleman raised was that we had acquired properties and then later on disposed of them. When they become surplus and we do not need to use them for years to come, we generally declare them surplus and they are handed over to the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation for disposal. Then we get rid of them and they are disposed of by this crown corporation. But still we hold on, in nearly every part of the country, to the properties that we own, because in the future we think we will need the sites or the buildings. When there are buildings on them we do rent them. But section 39 of the Public Works Act, which the hon. gentleman read, has this redeeming
TMr. Fournier (Hull).]
feature: "unless it is otherwise ordered by the governor in council." That is where I receive my power to rent.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext: That is, to rent your own buildings.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext:
To rent our old buildings. We have some of these properties in this city and in the country. We do receive requests from different people to rent. We do not ask tenders. We fix the rental price on the buildings we have to rent. During the war we were frozen, like everybody else, and we are still frozen, with people living in our buildings. When the controls disappear probably we shall follow the trend, make an assessment and value of these rentals and charge that price. The people renting these properties are not the roving kind. They stay put. We have far more difficulty in getting them out when we need the building than they have to pay the rent. I have an instance right here in Ottawa where I have been held up for four or five years because, on account of the shortage of housing in Ottawa we dare not tell these people to get out.
Even if we were to ask for tenders we would not ask these people to overbid the rentals for houses. Perhaps we would receive high rentals that would not be in line with the rentals the private owners had asked. With the controls I do not know whether I would be empowered to have people bidding on these properties.

I was not complaining about government buildings which the minister no longer needs and is therefore renting. I merely cited section 39 to show that even in such cases there is provision made either for tender or rental by auction or sale by auction, and with public advertising. The minister said that a department such as the post office would come to him and say: "We want to rent No. 50 Main street."

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext: It would not go out as definite as that.

minister's department. Somehow, the supporters of the government are finding out that there is a postal station required in a certain area and they have been able to get the lease.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext: No.

In fact in cases of this kind the department would have been wiser to build its own buildings rather than let somebody chisel in by finding out that there was going to be a building and then picking up property and getting a loan from the bank to put up the building and ending up with a nice government lease without any competition. I believe in that principle, and my officials have been instructed to that effect. But the hon. gentleman is going back to some years in which we could not get space or put up space. Hon. members will recall that a special commission was appointed, consisting of Brigadier A. Theriault and Mr. Edouard Laurent, to investigate the situation. They have prepared a report of their investigation, addressed to both governments, and I should like to table copies thereof. Following the production of the report I had discussions with the premier of Quebec. I should like to table a copy of a telegram I received from him late yesterday afternoon expressing the understanding reached with respect to relief to be extended in those two localities.
The report shows that at Rimouski the damage, exclusive of that incurred by Price Brothers and Company who operated a large mill at that place, amounted to $10,773,400, not including any damage to personal
3724	HOUSE OF
Rimouski and Cabano Fires property other than equipment of commercial firms used in the exploitation of their respective businesses. Against that there was fire insurance amounting to $2,120,400, leaving a loss of $8,653,000, of which the loss of individuals amounted to $3,715,000, partly covered by $1,250,000 of insurance, leaving a net for real property loss to individuals of $2,465,000.
The loss to institutions consisting of schools, hospitals, old people's home and the like amounted to $5,124,400 against which there was insurance of $775,400, leaving a net balance of $4,349,000. The loss incurred by utilities amounted to $204,000. In addition there was the value of a bridge completely destroyed, which is listed in the report as provincial property but which in fact was the property of the town of Rimouski. The commissioners were under the impression that the bridge had been taken over as part of a provincial highway, but such is not the case yet in the province of Quebec. Links between stretches of provincial highway which go through cities and towns are still the responsibility of the local authorities. Therefore the municipality and the utilities show a loss of $679,000.
These three net amounts total $7,493,000, practically seven and a half million dollars. In addition there was damage to federal property amounting to $260,000, according to the estimate, and to provincial property amounting to $930,000, according to the same estimate.
The situation in Cabano is that no special account was taken of the damage to the municipality, which was not very considerable. There was some damage to highways and sidewalks, but that was not brought into the calculation. There the damage suffered by individuals, excluding the Fraser Company Limited, amounted to $1,250,000, against which there was insurance amounting to $425,000, leaving a net of $825,000. The provincial government has appointed two local rehabilitation committees, both of them consisting of the commissioners who made the investigation, and in addition Mr. Paul Emile Gagnon in the case of Rimouski, and Mr. Emilien Morin, the mayor of Cabano, in the case of that town, to handle rehabilitation.
The telegram which I have filed covering the tentative understanding arrived at indicates that it is the intention of the provincial government to turn over to the Rimouski rehabilitation committee the sum of $2,500,000, and to turn over to the Cabano relief committee the sum of $300,000, to be applied to the rehabilitation of these localities. The tentative understanding is that the federal government will contribute equal amounts to (Mr. St. Laurent.]

both local committees. It is my understanding that the Minister of Finance will include an item in the supplementary estimates to provide the funds required.
In reading the telegram hon. members will see that there is a reservation made with respect to a marine technical school that had been erected in Rimouski at the joint expense of the provincial and federal governments for the training of seamen. They will see it is not to be taken into account in the allocation of the relief amounts provided by the sums I have mentioned, but that its reconstruction is to be the subject of further negotiations between the federal and provincial governments.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my constituents, who suffered such a calamity at Cabano, I wish to thank the Prime Minister, the members of the government and all my colleagues of the House of Commons for their generous sympathy in the terrible disaster. The Prime Minister took the trouble to go to Cabano. He saw the people there, and I am sure that he admired the dignity they displayed in their misfortune. We needed co-operation and action, and we have had both. I am most happy that there has been so much co-operation between the federal and provincial governments to help the people concerned in order that they may rebuild their houses before next fall.
I thank the gentlemen who were appointed by both governments to make a survey. I thank all those who have been generous enough to give a helping hand to so many people who suffered at Cabano and Rimouski. I thank the provincial government for having organized a trust fund, and the Star and La Presse for having given such wide publicity to it. I must not forget the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Houde), his worship the mayor of Montreal, and the members of the municipal council of that city, who have made a generous donation and have organized a concert at the Forum in aid of those in such distress.
I could not possibly enumerate all those who have done something to show a real understanding of human suffering and a true spirit of fraternity. I thank the Prime Minister in the first place and all those who have shown themselves so generous and so truly Canadian in helping their fellow citizens who were the victims of such a calamity.

Others in the district feel the same way. I suggest that from my personal observation there is a shortage of engineering staff in British Columbia. I might add that the officials have excellent public relations with representative public bodies and with the public generally. I believe they have shown very good judgment in dealing with the situations that have arisen in connection with the work of the department in that province.
Before passing on to the main subject with which I want to deal let me say a word about dredging on the Arrow lakes. I want to express the appreciation of the people of the district for the excellent work done by the dredge on those lakes within the past year. There has been excellent cooperation between the captain of the dredge and the captain of those vessels operating on the lakes. While this year, as the minister will be able to judge from an examination of the report, the yardage does not appear to be as high as in former years, excellent work has been done in deepening the channel to make the navigation of the river easier for those who use it.
Mr. Chairman, I rose particularly to deal with the policy concerning riverbank erosion and river wall protection. Representing as I do, in common with the member for Kamloops, a constituency touching on the Columbia river, I am concerned about the possibility of flood damage at Trail which is imminent at the present time, and the damage from erosion that has occurred at certain spots throughout the year. This was brought forcibly to my attention, in the first place, through the 1948 flood when the city of Trail suffered heavy damage as a result of the overflowing of the Columbia river at various points. t An appeal was made to the minister by the city council. I have a copy of their petition presented here and it deals with the difficulties to be faced and what is required to remedy them. I discussed the matter with the minister, his deputy minister
[Mr. Herridge.l

and some of his engineers. I quite agree with the reply the minister made to that request. As I understand it, there is a constitutional angle to the question. The waters, so far as navigation is concerned, are the property of the federal government; so far as power production is concerned, they are the property of the province. It is the kinetic energy in the water that produces the power; it is the kinetic energy that erodes the banks of the river. Therefore it was the property of the province destroying the property of the province. The minister suggested the city should apply to the province, and the province should make application to the federal authorities for some assistance to build a river wall. I support that proposal. I think that is quite sound. We cannot have every village, city and municipality dealing with the dominion government. The proper chain of responsibility is from the municipality to the province, from the province to the federal government.
Unfortunately, the provincial government took no action in this matter. A resolution was brought before the provincial legislature, but it was withdrawn on the promise of the minister to deal with the situation. He said he would bring it unofficially to the attention of the federal minister. No purpose is served by bringing a matter unofficially to the attention of a representative of another government, so nothing has happened.
Erosion has been a problem on the Columbia river ever since British Columbia entered confederation. Upon examining the correspondence and documents of that time, I find that it first arose in 1890, and later in 1892 when a petition was presented to the federal government to have something done to prevent the erosion of the river bank near Revelstoke. Then the provincial legislature of British Columbia passed a resolution in 1894 urging the federal government to assist the province with the problem of the erosion of the Columbia river bank. In 1900 some $33,000 was spent as a result of this resolution and the federal government bore half of the cost.
It has been a problem throughout the years, although the dangerous possibilities were not brought to the attention of the people in recent years until the flood of 1948. In going through the correspondence it appears to me that the federal government has made certain grants to the provincial government for Columbia riverbank protection. I understand that today the federal government takes the stand it will do riverbank protection work in order to protect its own structures or in order to repair some

damage occasioned by a structure of the dominion government or some work of the dominion government or for navigation. I think I am correct in that. If the city of Trail, which is a vital city so far as Canada is concerned, is to be adequately protected it will require at least $1 million to extend the city river wall to the city limits. That is necessary work if Trail is to be properly protected.
In addition to that there are other minor works that should be undertaken along the river. I believe some extensive riverbank protection work is required at Revelstoke, but I believe the member for Kamloops will deal with that later. It is about time, Mr. Chairman, that we had a policy with respect to riverbank protection and erosion. It seems to me there is no defined policy, and the government continues to dawdle over the whole question. There is no policy or no plan laid down to meet this urgent situation facing the cities and communities lying along the banks of our great rivers. There is a job to be done in the protection of those communities. At the same time there will be men who will be unemployed next winter, and who will require employment. I am not going to take the time of the house, Mr. Chairman, to go into the full details. I could say much more.

cent on request, I think it would help many of these smaller men who tender on these jobs.
I should like to remind the hon. member for Kootenay West that the Columbia river is not the only one that is eroding in Canada. The Red river is causing considerable damage to market gardeners. As to many of the market gardens along that river, as much as 50 to 100 feet of land have drifted into the river during the last 15 to 20 years. The Winnipeg river is causing considerable damage at the present time. [DOT] I believe it is higher now than it has been at any time since 1916, and it extends possibly one and a half feet over the road which runs from Lac du Bonnet to Pine Falls, which is the main road. I have been asked by several of these people along the Red river, as well as by people along the Winnipeg river, if something can be done to curb this erosion which is taking place year after year. I will ask the minister and his department to see whether they can work out something definite to help those people.

I just want to support what the hon. member for Kootenay West has said with regard to erosion. I always let him take the lead in this matter because more of the Columbia river lies in his constituency than in mine, although in mine lies the most valuable and attractive part of the river. As a matter of fact, I had a telegram just today from Revelstoke on this very problem of erosion. I did not like to bother the minister personally because he is here with his estimates, but his departmental officials are looking into it.
I should like to support to the full what the hon. member for Kootenay West has said to the effect that there is no clear-cut policy. The localities, the municipalities and the individual areas affected do not know whether to look to their federal member or to the provincial member; and between the three divided authorities, we do not seem to get very far. In justice I should pause here to echo what the hon. member preceding me has said. I think that the federal government has gone quite far in discharging the responsibilities which are unquestionably its own. There is no complaint on that score. When it can be clearly shown that it is a federal responsibility, they have come in and have done considerable bank protection work at Revelstoke, which has been of great value in that area. But then again that was where it was the result of previous federal construction or was an interference with navigation. But in the great majority of cases where

there is no clear-cut division of responsibility, where it cannot be clearly shown that it is the result of some federal construction or threat to navigation but is on a navigable stream, no one quite knows to whom to look.
It is something which is obviously beyond the resources of the municipality to handle. The provincial authorities say that it is a navigable stream and that the federal government should co-operate, and the federal government take the position that it is not an interference with navigation and therefore it is not their responsibility. I feel that if, as a result of discussions, we could have a clear-cut policy on this whole question of erosion, which is of importance not only on the Columbia but on the Thompson and the north Thompson in the rest of my riding and further down the Fraser as well, then those areas affected might expect to have some progress. I believe that the proper basis would be a joint contribution by the municipalities, the province and the federal authorities to deal with this question of bank erosion.
In conclusion, I just want to impress upon the minister the fact that it is a matter of some urgency because every year acres of valuable land are falling prey to the encroachment of this constant erosion by the rivers in the flood seasons of the year.

I have just one brief
question to ask the minister. In the past year we had quite heavy unemployment in the winter months, and I suppose we shall have it again next winter. The Prime Minister and others have suggested that it is seasonal unemployment. I wonder if it would be feasible for the Department of Public Works to do more of their building in the winter months when the construction industry is slack. I know that, in my own city, hospitals have been built in that way. Once they got the outer shell up, the men worked inside. It seems to me that might be a tangible step which this department might take to alleviate seasonal unemployment in the winter. I should like to know whether the minister thinks it is feasible or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
With regard to that
last question, the Public Works Act does not contemplate that we put up engineering or architectural works in order to relieve unemployment. You must admit that if you read the act. That is not the object of the Public Works Act. It is to put up these works to meet the needs of the different services in the country. We do our utmost to proceed the year round with buildings. In British Columbia we have work going on the year round. But you cannot do that in other provinces of the country. I do not think that I could give any other answer than that,

unless more authority were given to me, to try to relieve unemployment, and it were made one of the duties of my department that, regardless of the cost, I could undertake work just to relieve unemployment.

Of course, if you do not do
something like that in the winter, you are paying out unemployment insurance anyway. It does seem to me that even if it cost a little bit more to build in the winter, with regard to inside work at least it would be a way of alleviating seasonal unemployment in many parts of Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I wish to deal with the broad
question of how the Department of Public Works fits into the over-all picture of construction of government buildings and the way in which it would seem to me that this subject might well be examined before we are called upon once again to consider estimates. As to this year, I recognize that we are necessarily committed to the pattern of estimates that we have before us and to the general procedure that has been followed. This, however, seems to be the appropriate point at which to make certain observations which I should think might well be given careful consideration by the members of this committee in examining what is happening in connection with the construction of public buildings.
When the hon. member for Fort William expressed his concern about the increasing fat which he had noticed in some places-and he, with his usual politeness, did not indicate any particular place-I was conscious of the fact that there are also other places where there is a certain amount of fat appearing, and places other than on the human frame. One of the things about which all of us must think perhaps more than we have been called upon to think in the past is the extent to which the budgets for every requirement of government are becoming fatter and fatter and, in that very process, are imposing increasing tax burdens upon every taxpayer in Canada.
One of the difficulties of offering any suggestions as to places where savings can be made or otherwise is that in the very nature of things it is only those who are dealing with each of the problems who can possibly know whether or not there might have been certain economies which would have maintained efficiency and conceivably even increased efficiency. But one of the things that do strike one rather forcibly is this. In the year before the war the total figure called for in the estimates of the Department of Public Works was $14,560,749. The amount called for this year for the acquisition or construction of buildings, works and structures is $61,431,500. I am not prepared to say, nor
Supply-Public Works
am I in a position to say, that included in these figures are not figures that indicate inefficiency or otherwise. We are simply presented with the information as to the buildings that are to be erected, and what they will cost.
What I would point out, however, is that not all the buildings that are being constructed by the government are being built by the Department of Public Works; and that in addition to the buildings that are being acquired or constructed by the Department of Public Works are buildings that are being acquired or constructed by other departments as well.
In a recent summary of a total figure in the estimates for the acquisition or construction of buildings, works and structures, prepared by Mr. Bryce, we find that the total over-all figure for this year will be $168,575,705 as compared with $35,830,565 in the last year before the war. That is a very large increase; and again we see that buildings are being constructed by departments which were not assuming the responsibility for constructing buildings in the fiscal year 1938-39. For instance, in the present estimates we find that the Department of National Health and Welfare has items for buildings to the amount of $2,311,250; Resources and Development, $13,482,390; Veterans Affairs, $4,535,000; National Revenue, $427,000.
In these instances I have mentioned only departments which built nothing separately as departments in 1938-39, the last fiscal year before the war. There are other departments like National Defence which were carrying on construction in the year before the war. Let us take a comparison there. In the last year before the war the amount was $4,261,050. This year the amount estimated is $36,265,257. In the case of Transport it was $7,324,389 in the year before the war. This year the estimates call for $20,410,816. I have given these last figures only to show that in department after department, where construction is taking place, there is this very large proportionate increase. It seems to me that when we are confronted with the comparative figures for all acquisition or construction of buildings, works and structures, by different departments of government-and this of course is entirely exclusive of the crown corporations and different ventures of various kinds-we find that the comparative figures are $35,830,565 the year before the war, and $168,575,705 today. It does seem that we at least should consider whether it would not be wise that there should be some more effective over-all supervision of construction, and perhaps some uniform plan of construction

Supply-Public Works
which might effect economies which otherwise would be overlooked because of the fact that these things would be done separately.
I recall as an example only one item that came before us for construction and it was a school that was being built in northern Canada, where in one of the departments the plans were obtained for a school of certain value. The architect was paid the fee for that plan. Then it was decided that they did not want quite so large a school. New plans were drawn and the architect was paid fees for the second plan as well. I merely mention this as one item that came up for consideration in the accounts this year, to show that there are places where a careful examination and one uniform system of supervision might well disclose places where savings could be made in this very large figure.
Under the Department of Public Works there is a strict requirement in regard to the calling for tenders. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has referred to the situation that arose in Vancouver, and I do not intend to enlarge upon it beyond this. The device that was employed there could be one that would circumvent the intended restrictions in the act under which this department operates. The facts speak for themselves. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has put these facts forward. The minister has given his explanation, and I do not intend to extend the discussion which has been so fully covered. I would point out, however, that if it were intended to circumvent these restrictions, what was done in that particular case-and I refer to what has been known as the Alvin building-could be a method to avoid the ordinary requirements; because, where the government intended to buy, it could arrange to buy but nevertheless in advance to arrange a lease with a purchase option and in the process avoid the necessity of calling for tenders, and then subsequently take up the option, and by that means avoid the intended protection of the calling for tenders.
I am putting this forward only to indicate that a method of this kind could be abused if it became an extended practice.
Perhaps, however, what has happened in this case does suggest the very great desirability of an over-all review by competent, outside experts as to the way in which the whole program of construction is carried on, not only by this but by all government departments, so that every advancement in construction methods and every practical economy that has been discovered as a result of the great building developments of the past few years may be applied to the construction of government buildings of all kinds.

Without impropriety of any kind, and without hint or suggestion of impropriety it nevertheless must suggest itself to every hon. member that practices which go on year after year, without any independent examination, in the experience of every one of us do almost invariably lead to the acceptance of methods which might be improved if they were checked and examined from time to time.
What is happening here is only one of the reasons that I did urge an over-all examination of the whole business of government by an independent royal commission. That has been dealt with, and I shall not extend the discussion of that suggestion at this session. But I do most earnestly put before the minister for consideration the advisability of a thorough consideration of the whole procedure in connection with the construction of public buildings, not only in his own department, but in all departments of government which are now building to the extent of $168 million a year. Those figures are so large that they are almost beyond the understanding of many people. Sometimes figures become so large that we are inclined to become less careful in their examination than when they are in terms we understand in our daily contacts.
With the figures before us it is not possible for members of the House of Commons to say, "You could save $1,000 here", or "You could save $10,000 in this item" or "You might save $50,000 in that item". That is not possible. We do not examine these as architects or as building engineers. They are put before us as jobs that should be done-and let me say at once that in most, if not in all cases, they are jobs that do need to be done. Members want to have them done in a way that will impose the least possible burden of taxation upon the taxpayer.
My remarks have been general for the very reason I have indicated, namely that we cannot examine in detail. But I do suggest that the enormous increase in the cost of building which in the year before the war was $35 million to the present figure of $168 million, should be a warning, a signal, that the time has come to review the method by which these arrangements are made, and to see if there are not economies which could be practised, either in the matter of buying, different plans of construction, or otherwise.
May I point out in relation to the activities of this department that there is a clear indication of the way in which costs are rising when we look at the item for maintenance and repairs. In the year before the war the Department of Public Works was shown as

spending $3,664,294 on maintenance and repairs in the estimates for that year. This year under the same heading there is an amount of $33,551,248. In other words the figure for this year is almost ten times what it was the year before the war. May I add that the figures I have used in each case are those supplied by Mr. Bryce in what was described as a functional breakdown of the over-all estimates of the different departments, under the heading "acquisition or construction of buildings, works and structures."
I shall conclude with the repeated request that the minister take this into consideration and do what any ordinary business concern would do, namely bring in the best available advice to make sure that if there are any ways in which savings can be made they will be undertaken.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is not every day that I would be ready to compliment the leader of the opposition upon a speech; but today he has certainly impressed me with the study he has made of these figures concerning the Department of Public Works, and other departments.
May I in a few words place before him the little experience I have gained since I have been Minister of Public Works. In 1942-43 when I was first appointed, according to the figures given me by my officials we had an appropriation of $18,221,351. At that time we were at war, and it was found that the statute under which we operated was so restrictive that it took us a good deal of time to get results. In street parlance, one would say, "There is too much red tape in public works."
I have to admit that this is one of the oldest departments of government. It is built on experience, people having joined it when they were very young, and having grown up with it and received their training from older officials. I become impatient when I bring down my estimates and there are revotes. Well, it has been explained to me that they do not run; they just walk and go slowly to avoid mistakes.
So, during the war, instead of giving all the construction work to the Department of Public Works, other departments were set up. Some of the departments handed their work to this other department which, at the time, was the department of munitions and supply. For instance, the Department of Veterans Affairs, which had always had an engineering and architects branch, would have construction done by the Department of National Defence. It developed that people avoided the Department of Public Works, because we did not get results. We could not go fast enough-and I think their action was proper
Supply-Public Works
at the time. But to get those quick results one could not follow the statute exactly, and we operated under the statute.
This condition grew up during the war. There is no doubt about it that some departments were not always satisfied with the way we gave them space or the works they wanted. Departments were growing rapidly and we were confronted by a number of regulations under which priorities for materials and labour were given to other departments.
So you see our estimates during the war years were kept very low-$18,021,351, and then in the next year $21,464,304, and then going back to $20,346,734 in 1944-45, and then up to $23,178,041. But we have to admit that since the war I have been pressing the government to go ahead with works. In 1946 nearly everything that belonged to the government by way of public works was deteriorating to the extent that we were losing some of those works. So I insisted that I receive amounts sufficient at least to try to repair, maintain or rebuild. As to maintenance and repairs, I have received some votes, but in the last two years, when the situation eased as to materials and there was more labour on the market, I convinced them that we should undertake new projects and buildings. In that process I had to rebuild the staff of the Department of Public Works. When I became minister in 1942 it was around 4,000 and it now approximates 7,400.
There is a lot in the thought of the leader of the opposition that there might be a saving if we could concentrate all building for every department in the Department of Public Works. I do not say there would be, but we would have to increase the staff of the department to quite an extent to handle the surplus of $60 million worth of works that are done outside the Department of Public Works. I think the proper procedure is that when the need for works is demonstrated to the satisfaction of the officials of the department, the community, members of parliament and the government, then we should undertake those works, following the statute as closely as humanly possible. We have been trying to do that.
One case was cited where perhaps we may have deviated and tried to avoid the provisions of the law. I will tell you candidly that was never the intention. I am not going to give all the reasons that I have given in the house before. It was never the intention to avoid the law. The purpose was to try to get quickly something that was required by departments. That was the only reason that motivated me in that instance. I do not think we made a bad job of it, but I do not

Supply-Public Works
believe in the principle. If we are going to start abandoning the system of asking for tenders we do not know where a government would stop. We have examples all over the country. Although I do not pose as a model, I believe in the tender system because we are spending everybody's money, and everybody has a chance to tender to make money out of these contracts. While I am head of the department I would not want any change in the system, and I will try to see that does not take place.
As to the increase in the estimates, it is not only because of the number of works but also the cost of materials and labour. We just grew up with the other departments of government. In 1939 we only had 12,000 or 13,000 civil servants in the city of Ottawa, and today I believe we have over 40,000. It takes a lot of space to provide for that number of employees if you want them to have an average of 85 square feet per employee, although I think the normal should be 100. It takes a lot of space to provide conditions of work comparable to those in industry. Requests come in to provide better conditions of work in every city so that they will be on an1 equal footing with industry and business generally. If you do that the expenditure will be very large.
During the war, employees worked in 55 to 60 square feet of space per person. I think the average has gone up to around 80 or 85, but it really should be about 100 square feet. I know it is difficult to discuss the details of the public works estimates. If I meet someone I can give him the proceedings and details in conversation. In the house that would be quite a job although I would undertake to do so if the session lasted all year. In a session lasting only for some months of the year it would be quite difficult.
Although I do not know if I can carry it out, I will certainly consider seriously the proposal to have construction concentrated in my department. Circumstances may arise where my department might not be able to fill the bill at all unless we change the statute to give me more leeway, and really I would not want to be minister of the department unless we had the controls in the Public Works Act. I do not know what would happen to a man who would undertake to handle this business without having the straight principles laid1 down in the act, and I do not think I would be the proper man to administer the department under those circumstances.
Coming back to the officials of the department, I think I have about the best staff trained in different branches of the work

that could be had. I will not say they are perfect, but you would be surprised to know all the details that enter into their reports before they make a recommendation to the minister. I could mention the heads of the architectural and engineering divisions in the fifteen different districts, and every name I would give you would be that of an outstanding man in his field in that particular district. They have experience and they know the local situation. They are well trained. They were educated in universities all over Canada and outside this country.
When a community sends a delegation or makes a request for a building or works of some kind I try to meet their wishes as much as possible. My immediate contact is with members of parliament on every side of the house. I do not know of one member who has come to my office to see me to explain a situation that I have not given serious consideration to the matter. In any event, you can look at the estimates and you will see that I have tried not to play favourites as to public works. I do not believe in that. I do not believe it is a good thing for the country. I do not believe it is a good way to spend the people's money. If a member of parliament comes to me with a serious project I have a report made on it by my engineers or architects. I have the advice of the gentlemen seated in front of me today. Then I am ready to go before the government or treasury board and try to get an estimate through. The moment the money is voted it falls back on the department and its officials to prepare plans, specification, estimates and ask for tenders.
We do not generally ask for public tenders for small works under $5,000. We ask for tenders from known firms in the community. In all other cases we ask for public tenders. It has been said that contracts are not always awarded to the lowest tenderer. The explanation I gave a moment ago is the only reason for that that I can see. I have in mind the case where an accepted cheque does not accompany the tender, and the tender is thrown out and not considered. If a tender does not meet the specifications it is thrown out. In certain instances when we have had dealings with contractors who have fallen down on contracts which we have had to complete we look into the capabilities and organization of such firms whenever they tender again. We do not turn down the lowest tenders. They are accepted except under the circumstances I have outlined. If anybody thinks I have made a mistake in that statement and can produce a case I should like to see the file myself. I would be sorry to see that it had escaped

my attention because I look at all these tenders that come to my desk and try to give them all the attention I can.
Coming back to the subject that started this discussion, remedial works, there is no set policy, but I think the hon. member for Kamloops has grasped the situation as to what we do in cases of damage by erosion. When there has been a clear-cut responsibility on the part of the federal government I think we have met the emergency and have proceeded with the works. In other cases of flood conditions throughout the country we would not touch the damages caused by flood. The best example is the Fraser river catastrophe. When it happened the government undertook to pay not 100 per cent but 75 per cent of the cost of the dikes or protection works. Probably we will soon make an agreement with the province of Manitoba if they wish to construct dikes, but there are circumstances where we do not think that is our responsibility. Right across the river, in my own riding, there happens to be a river that nearly every year floods part of a village known as Gatineau Point. Each year a number of homes in that village will be flooded to the extent that the people will have to go out of the second storey windows and into their little rowboats in order to get to work; still they want to continue to live there. For ten years as a member of this house I tried to get the Minister of Public Works to put up some protection works in that area, but I did not succeed; nor have I been able to succeed in having that done since I have been the minister myself. There are still no protection works at that point.
I do not know what should be done. The idea has been expressed, and it has a good deal to it, that the province and the federal government might come to an understanding as to the proportion of the cost to be paid on such works. I believe that would be all to the good, but just think of the amount of money that would have to be spent for this purpose every year. As hon. members know, floods occur all over the country, and if we were to carry on this work certainly it would have to be done gradually, because I do not believe the budget of my department would be sufficient to meet the cost.
At the moment we were dealing mainly with erosion, which is not due to an unusual or catastrophic flood but which merely occurs at the high water season each year.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Quite so. We do
take steps when this damage is caused by some of our works, or to our works, or by navigation. In those cases we generally take action after the report is received, and we
Supply-Public Works
will continue to do that until agreements are made with the provinces concerning those works, if that should come about.

Has the government of British Columbia or any member of it approached the minister or his department concerning assistance in connection with the construction of protection walls on the Columbia river?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My official tells me that the hon. member who just spoke did approach us in connection with those works, but he has no knowledge of any other representation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not want to discuss this point further, beyond emphasizing something that has been brought out by the minister himself. He points out that he would not want to carry on a program of public works without the protection afforded by the act. It is protection for the public, for the minister and for his officials.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Don't try to make me blame someone else.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am not suggesting that at all. I am pointing out that in this particular case we have reached the point where the work done by the Department of Public Works, which in the mind of the public and really in the minds of members of this house is the great construction department, amounts to $31,431,500, while the building done by other departments, which in the ordinary course of events are not supposed to be great construction departments, amounts to $107,124,205. In those cases they are not subject to the same requirements and we know of many cases-though how many we are unable to say-in which these works have been done without calling for tenders.
Knowing that we cannot change the presentation of these estimates at this time I can only leave the matter by repeating the request that the minister give earnest consideration to the desirability of placing before the government the suggestion that, except in unusual cases, the general construction program be brought together and placed under the same requirements which protect both the government and the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I would not like to follow the leader of the opposition the whole way. Only yesterday we passed the Defence Supplies Act, which gives powers that are not contained in the Public Works Act; and they were put in that act for special reasons. In circumstances where the defence of my country would justify action without following this procedure, I would not want to be

Supply-Public Works
committed to that procedure; but I am talking of ordinary works, buildings and other facilities, that are to be constructed. I could not undertake even to do the work that is being done by the national harbours board. They have special authority to do that work. When I say I would not like to act as minister under an act that would not give the public and myself and my officials that protection, I am concerned with the buildings that come under our jurisdiction. I would like to have this protection in connection with anything we undertake.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Just to keep the arithmetic straight I would point out that the entire national defence estimate for construction for the current year is $36,265,257, which still leaves $70,858,948 of construction under other departments. This is substantially more than the total called for under the minister. I am going to leave the figures at that point, simply as part of my argument that this whole subject should be reviewed.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is true, as the hon. member says, that the figure is quite large. The explanation I have here, which was given by Mr. Bryce though I had not seen it before, is that this amount includes provision for all expenditures on new construction of buildings, roads-we do not build roads-irrigation works, canals, airports, wharves-which we do build-bridges or other types of fixed assets. It includes major improvements and renovations involving changes of a structural nature, and also the installed cost of fixed equipment which is an essential part of the structure, such as elevators, heating and ventilating equipment. I do not think we would have the organization to undertake many of these things. Certainly I would not have the staff to look after these irrigation projects, which account for quite a large expenditure each year. As to anything that we ordinarily do in the department, however, I should like to see everyone follow the procedure that we have adopted.

A few moments ago the minister said he did not believe in playing favourites in connection with public works. With that I entirely agree, and I do not think he does play favourites. When we were discussing his estimates last year, however, I drew his attention to the rather peculiar circumstance that the ridings of Liberal members in Newfoundland apparently were getting a much greater expenditure on public works than were the other ridings, and at that time I believe the minister agreed that it was a rather peculiar coincidence. I do not know the position under the present estimates; I have asked for the information, but have not been given any details as yet. Would the

minister tell me briefly, riding by riding, what expenditures are to be made in Newfoundland this year? Then I may be in a better position to discuss the matter.
Before resuming my seat I have one or two other matters to mention. One rather important matter is the question of a public federal building. I understand one or two such buildings are scheduled for St. John's, and one of the sites suggested is the grounds of government house. I want to protest against that, in case any such decision should be made. I think that would be a very improper place for such a building, and certainly it would not be welcomed at all by the citizens of St. John's.
I will take it over in my riding.

I think you are getting enough now. The other important matter is the question of the wharf at Portugal Cove. At first glance that may appear to toe a minor point, but it is the terminal for Bell island, where we have the ore mine which has been in operation for the past fifty years. The people of Bell island, numbering some ten thousand, depend upon that wharf for everything they need, including all their food and clothing. Everything must pass over it. Perhaps I may be pardoned for saying that it is possibly the busiest wharf on the island of Newfoundland, in the sense of daily use. The wharf is in very bad condition at the present time. There appears to be some difference between the provincial authorities and your own department about who is going to undertake the repairs. I believe you have been informed of that matter. I am told that the provincial minister has written to you concerning it, and your deputy minister is fully aware of the condition. It is a serious matter. If the wharf is allowed to continue to deteriorate it will not be usable, and those people in that thriving and important community which supplies a great deal of iron ore will be in a serious situation. I plead with the minister that, whoever is going to be responsible for the repairs, something be done immediately.
There is some difference over the fact that a ferry is using the wharf part of the time, and therefore it should be entirely a provincial matter. I know from my own knowledge, because the wharf is in my riding, that a number of fishermen and schooners use it as well, so it is hardly just a ferry wharf. Whoever is responsible for the repair should do the work as quickly as possible or there will be a lot of unfortunate people in that community.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I understand that Portugal Cove is a repair job, and that will be taken care of. The hon. member has

written to the department about the other information, and I understand we received the letter yesterday. The department is preparing an answer, and we will send it as soon as possible.

Last year
in the supplementary estimates there were votes 704 to 709, and I wonder if the minister is in a position to say how much of those votes was spent in Newfoundland?

speechtext: We spent the $211,000 there.
