speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
When this vote came
up last year it was for the extension of the service throughout the country, including
Supply-Public Works
Newfoundland. I have given the amount we spent, except the salaries, because I have not that list here.
The dredging of harbours and rivers: you have not given me that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext: How much was spent on harbours and rivers generally?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That was the $370,000, in round figures.
Mr. Chairman, I do not think the minister really understands the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Last year when we had the million dollar vote for harbours and rivers, that estimate was prepared just as Newfoundland came into the union. We had no idea what staff would be needed there, so we had to have a round figure without knowing exactly what we would spend. Out of that estimate we did spend $370,000.

I still do not think the minister understands the question I am asking. In the supplementary estimates up to March 31, 1950, there are six votes totalling $3,620,000. The minister has given me three figures, and that is all. Two of those votes are for a million dollars. On one of them I have received no information. If it is not convenient to get the information now, perhaps we can get it when we come to the particular item.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Or else I shall ask my officials to look at Hansard, and send you the details about these votes.

Is the minister responsible
for the air conditioning of this building? If so, he is responsible for a rotten condition. I might just as well say so here as to say it outside. Anyone who sits in here very long, with the direct draught blowing on him, will get the same kind of a cold as some of the rest of us have. I think it would be as well to die of bad air as to die of this new virus cold.
At this point I should like to refer to the number of people employed by the department. I always thought that many of these temporaries were put on during an election year. The Department of Public Works seems to employ about 7,000 people.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is 6,600.

There are 1,568 permanents,
5,277 temporaries, and then this new group is included of about 400 casuals or "casualties", I do not know which. In any event there are over 7,000.

Supply-Public Works

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is correct.

I want to compliment the minister, because this is the first year we have been able to find out how many temporaries there were. We ought to find out now what salaries are received by these temporaries. Are they all on the same rate, which would appear to run around $2,100, or what is the rate? The amount paid totals over $7 million, which would give these temporaries an average wage of $1,650. We would like to know how many of them have been temporary for a long time. Why are they still temporary? If they are all new people put on each year, surely there is some way of giving them some form of security? If you are employing these people year after year, why not give them the same sense of security that permanent civil servants have? I have said enough about those things before, but I wanted to bring them to your attention again.
There is another matter to which I wish to refer, and we may have something to say on it somewhere else, but it must be in the administration. In the last five, six or possibly seven years we have been promised a public building, known as the Dominion building, for Charlottetown. In the 1945 election I know it was a wonderful promise to dangle before the city, especially the labour people, and it was well dangled at that time.
It worked.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You were elected just the same.
Certainly; they said they did not want it.

I barely got in. Five years afterwards it comes up again. There is no building built. However, I made a little bit better impression that time because I promised the electors faithfully I would get after it and get it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You are going to get it too.

There is no use in one side having it all. My colleague knew that he was going to be elected anyhow; and when I was promising to get this, it certainly helped me along. But we are no further ahead now. Here we are today in the position that in a certain part of the town the site has been selected, consisting of 24 or 25 properties, but I do not think any of them have been purchased yet unless a couple have been purchased lately. Now they are all in that court-what do you call it?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The exchequer court.

They are in the exchequer court, and they are having a real checker play

there. Properties in there belonging to some of the stalwarts of the party are valued as high as $100,000, which possibly cost in the beginning somewhere around $7,000 or $8,000 to build, and the land is extra. It will be amusing to see where these valuations are going to lead to. There is other property there, valued at $40,000, that I do not believe the minister would pay $8,000, $9,000 or $10,000 for it, any more than I would.
You could get the whole island for that.

However, there are other properties that are being valued too low, but I suppose the court will decide on that. What I want to know is this. How long is it going to take before we get a valuation on them so that the properties can be purchased and the building started? I am afraid that it will not start this year. In fact, I did not go home at Easter and that was one of the reasons. Now I am afraid to go home at the end of June. I should like to be able to say to the people in my constituency that the minister stood up in the house and said:	You are
going to get that building and you are going to have it started inside of the next three or four weeks. There is one thing they could do. They could get all the properties, pull them down and give employment to the hundreds of men who are idle there at the present time. I should like to hear the minister make a really good statement on that matter so that I can take it back with me.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will not be in a position to make as good a statement as the hon. member himself made.
You do not have to go home.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: At any rate, I have not made the same promises that he made. It is true that we have had this estimate up for some years; it is going to be a fine building, and it will be a credit to the two hon. members for Charlottetown. Our difficulty is that, after the site was chosen-and it comprised about 22 properties-we saw that the people out in the island valued their property highly. Perhaps they were sentimental values, but at all events they had put a high price on their properties. As I explained earlier, I would hesitate to go into dealings with people who have such a high idea of the values of their properties.
Too much sentiment.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The only recourse we have is to go to the court we mentioned, namely the exchequer court, where experts will represent the government and will give

the values we think attach to these properties; and the owners will have their own experts there to give evidence. I am sure that the judge will give the proper decision, and that amount will be paid. That is the real cause of this delay with regard to the building. But I would not despair if I were the hon. member. I would go home next week just the same and repeat the promise, because the building is coming; when, I do not know.

I wonder if the minister could give me an estimate of how much money is involved, in round figures, in this building he is discussing now? What I should like to do is to see how much it costs to buy a vote in Prince Edward Island.

I gather that
the properties are being expropriated and that is the reason you are in the exchequer court.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
Having expropriated, there is nothing to stop you from going ahead and doing your building, surely.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Quite so. But on the other hand, when I am forcefully taking property from people, I do not like to just throw them out. We have tried to deal with some of these people. When I was not satisfied with the other valuations, I have even sent people from Montreal in order to get a third valuation. I do not think we can come to an agreement. We shall have to get a judgment and pay the amount awarded by the court. There are businesses located in these buildings. I think one or two of the banks are located there. Just to go there without having a judgment and to say, "Get out" is something that I do not like to do. That is what makes me delay and try to get a judgment as soon as possible.

I want first to commend the Minister of Public Works and his department for the vote of money which he has given us for the renovation of the warehouse on the railway wharf at Souris and also for the appropriation for the dredging of the Montague river which is most necessary. It is necessary work and it had to be done to permit vessels to go up the Montague river and to load produce for Newfoundland, St. Pierre and other points.
In my riding of Kings county we have been asking the minister and his department for a considerably large vote of money for the renovation and extension of our wharf at Souris. I want to point out to the minister and his department that this is necessary work. I would hope that the minister would accept the plan proposed by Mr. H. E. Miller,
Supply-Public Works
our district engineer at Charlottetown. This plan provides for the extension of the present railway wharf-that is, the government wharf-and would provide room for a railway spur line that will enable smaller vessels to load at the wharf. At the present time we are unable to accommodate the smaller vessels because of the fact that in the heavy shipping season, which is in the fall and early spring, the large warehouse accommodates the larger vessels to be loaded for Bermuda and southern United States points, and we are unable to accommodate the smaller boats loading for Newfoundland, St. Pierre, Miquelon and Magdalen islands. If the department approves of that project and the railway wharf at Souris which we all believe is necessary, it would be a fine thing for the county of Kings, and unless we have that wharf extended and the wharf that was approved by the plan of the district engineer, it will be difficult for us to accommodate the shipping that would otherwise use that port of Souris. The port of Georgetown is also very important to the county of Kings. My people tell me that it is necessary to have the Queens wharf repaired and also the government railway wharf to accommodate the boats.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We have two items in the estimates for these works.
The Queens wharf and the Georgetown wharf?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: For Souris.
Yes, but I was wondering whether or not the minister approved in full the plan of the district engineer, Mr. Miller.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is quite a big plan.
Have you approved the plan or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We are considering it right now.
I do hope that you will approve Mr. Miller's plan.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Hope springs eternal.
Before taking my seat I wish to point out to the department-
Carried.

I have not taken up much of the time of the house during this session. I hear some members say "carried". I think I am entitled to a few words. In Kings county we have a large fishing industry. Many of our harbours are too shallow to give free access to the motorboats that fish for lobster, hake and cod. I should like to take

Supply-Public Works
this opportunity to impress upon the department the necessity of dredging harbour services for the north and south of my county.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Earlier this afternoon the Minister of Public Works, in answering a question of the hon. member for Moose Jaw, said, if I understood him correctly, that his department did not take into consideration the employment or unemployment situation when it came to public works.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You tell me what you did say.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not say that we did not take it into consideration. I said it was not the duty of public works to have estimates before the house to provide relief for unemployment. The estimates we have before parliament are for public works' needed by the public services of the country.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yes. The hon. member for Moose Jaw did not, today at any rate, suggest that money should be appropriated by public works just to provide work, but he was suggesting that the timing of public works might be made with a view to the unemployment situation.
May I remind the Minister of Public Works that in a sessional paper tabled on Wednesday, May 10, 1950, by his colleague the Minister of Resources and Development, this question was dealt with. To identify it, it is sessional paper No. 67J. It dealt with this question of mine:
What federal public works projects have been undertaken In order to relieve unemployment since September 1, 1949?
This was the answer of the minister's colleague, the Minister of Resources and Development:
The federal government's program of public investment, including public works, consists of worthwhile projects which will contribute toward the development of the country, and which can be implemented at such times as they will contribute to the maintenance of a high level of employment. In line with this policy, projects undertaken by all government departments since September 1, 1949, had full regard to the employment situation.
In that same connection, may I remind the Minister of Public Works that his department has contributed to another sessional paper No. 88D, tabled on Friday, June 2, 1950, in which information is given as to the money voted for public works over a period of a number of years, and not expended in each case during the year in which it was voted. I find that according to page 13 of this sessional paper the amount of money voted for public works projects for the Department of
[Mr. Kickham.j
Public Works which was not expended during the year seems to have been growing. In the year 1945-46 the amount voted but not expended during that year was $2,379,759.07; in the year 1946-47 it was $14 million odd; in the year 1947-48 it was $17 million odd; in the year 1948-49 it was $24 million odd; and for the fiscal year 1949-50 up until February 28, 1950, there was still $37,939,441.55 which had not been'expended.
I realize that these amounts are not sufficient to take care of the unemployment situation when it gets serious, but it does seem to me that there is. a possibility of dealing in part with unemployment problems if there was a little more co-ordination between what the Minister of Resources and Development says and what the Minister of Public Works does by way of making full use of the money that is voted for public works, and timing it to meet the needs of the unemployment situation.
I am not complaining about the large amounts of money being voted for public works projects; I am complaining of the fact that year by year the amount that is voted but not expended seems to be increasing.

289. Branch administration, $437,290.

I have one question on this item. Can the minister give us the total figure paid for the Alvin building in Vancouver? I believe that under the final terms of the option the price was to be $1,063,105; but in addition to that there were certain amounts paid as rental before this option was exercised, which by the way is a very unusual way to do business in Vancouver. Ordinarily the amount paid as rental would be applied on the purchase price when the option was exercised. I should like to get these two figures: First of all, the purchase price, and second the amount that was paid by way of rental, and which of course was lost to the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The cheque that was issued for that building amounted to $1,066,614.90. That is the amount paid to the Alvin estate.
In addition to that there were sums paid by way of rental before the option was exercised. I would like to get the aggregate of such payments.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I see that the rent was $183,995.
Per year?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. The order in council authorizing this was dated February 8, 1949, and the order in council with respect to the purchase of the building was dated March 15, 1950. That was just before the expiry date of the option. So that we must have paid rental for about a year or a little over a year on the property.
Perhaps the minister's officials could get that information and let me have it later.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes; I shall send it to the hon. member.
Because parts of the building were occupied before the whole building was completed, and the rent was payable on a pro rata basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, I understand.
So one could not reach the proper figure by simply taking the amount of the rental set out in the order in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I shall have the figure prepared for the hon. member.

291.	Maintenance and operation of dominion public buildings and grounds, other than at Ottawa, including rents, repairs, furniture, heating, etc., and to authorize commitments against future years in the amount of $500,000, $12,686,315.

What progress is being made in connection with the renovation and repair of the public building at Springhill in my constituency? This is a growing town, and one of the best maintained mining communities in all Canada. What progress is being made?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
This is not new
construction?
Renovation and repairing of a public building which has been there a good many years.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It would come out of our general vote.
It would come under item 291, would it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: But I have not the details of it here.
This vote involves an expenditure of more than $12 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My officials tell me they have not before them the details of the contract for decorating. However, we can send for a report on it and let the hon. member have it.

292.	Newfoundland, $455,000.
Is this for new buildings?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Gander is the only point where there is an addition to an existing building. I am told the others are new.
What is the public building at Bishop's Falls to be?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This is to provide for the construction of a public building for postal purposes. The post office at the present time is located in a privately-owned building which is old, small and poorly located. The Post Office Department requests the construction of a new building in category A. The Anglo-Newfoundland Development Company pulp mill has offered to donate a suitable site. Plans and specifications have not yet been completed.
Is it to be of wooden construction?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, it will be a fireproof building.
It will not be a very large one for that amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: So that the hon. member will understand, this amount which goes in the estimates for the first year is only for site, preparation of plans, asking for tenders and beginning works. I am sure we will never get through this building by March 31.

This is not intended to be the full amount?
* Mr. Fournier (Hull): No.
What is the value of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I cannot say before the plans and specifications are prepared.
Plans and specifications are not ready?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.
What about the building at Corner Brook?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This is to provide for the construction of a public building for post office, customs, transport, trade and commerce, labour, agriculture, R.C.M.P. and unemployment insurance.
And can the minister tell me where the postal terminal in St. John's is to be erected?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Along the railway siding, I am told.

And the other building there?

Supply-Public Works

We have not yet
chosen the site. One of our difficulties is to have agreement as to the site.

293.	Nova Scotia, $1,350,000.

A building for post office accommodation, at Pugwash, was suggested to the minister before, and he gave some encouragement. According to revenue received, it is one of the buildings in Nova Scotia most greatly needed. I notice that under this heading the appropriation for Nova Scotia is only $1,350,000. That is less per capita than in any other of the provinces of eastern Canada, with the exception of Newfoundland. I am not objecting to the larger appropriation for Prince Edward Island; but New Brunswick with only four-fifths of the population of Nova Scotia has an appropriation about a million dollars greater. What progress is the minister's department making in connection with the. public building at Pugwash?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We are studying the situation there to see if we can do something about it.

A few moments ago the hon.
member for Winnipeg North Centre, and others, referred to the relationship of the minister's department toward relieving unemployment conditions in Canada. I am particularly interested in the subject because it affects my constituency. The minister stated his department did not anticipate that there would be any projects designed for that particular purpose.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out that the Minister of Resources and Development took a different view. I was here when he made his statement, and I took some encouragement from it, because the department he represents is one which fluctuates. This department is a permanent department that works on public works projects year in and year out.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Under a statute.

Under a statute, but definitely they can create and promote necessary public works projects in sections that need them. So far as it is practical, I think they should design their activities to take care of sections where there is a bad permanent unemployment problem. The point I am getting at is that, in the return which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre just quoted to the minister concerning the appropriations made year by year to his department for certain works projects,

it shows that a lot of money has been voted to the minister's department for public works projects in Nova Scotia and has not been spent. The return sets it out year by year. It goes back to 1945-46, and runs all the way from $243,000 for Nova Scotia in 1945-46 to over $3 million in 1948-49.
In the final break-down of the return it shows that at February 28, 1950, the total amount was $4,200,469.99. That is quite a lot of money in a province that size. The money was appropriated and involved considerable work in the minister's department. Surveys had to be made for the purposes for which the money was voted. Taking a quick look at the estimates for 1949 it appears that some $7 million or $8 million was voted to the minister's department for works projects in the province of Nova Scotia, but at February 5, 1950, half of that money was still unspent.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: When was it voted, what date?
It was voted all the way from 1945 to 1949 and not spent. It accumulated to the figure I have given. The return shows that you owe the province of Nova Scotia over $4 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh no. Do not confuse that. On the 10th of December, 1949, we voted the whole amount of the estimates. From the 10th of December, 1949, to the 31st March, 1950, we did not spend the amount voted. There was $3 million that we could not spend during the wintertime on these works. You know that we cannot work on wharves and breakwaters in Nova Scotia during the wintertime.
I still contend that you owe us $4 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If we owe you something we will pay it.

Your department made surveys as to projects which are badly needed in that province. After all the work of putting the appropriations through and arguing about them, then you do not spend the money because winter comes along and you let the work lapse. What is your intention with regard to-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: They are good.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It was ever thus.

What is the intention with regard to carrying on the works projects involved in the amount of $4 million that has not been spent? Is it your intention to go ahead with these projects and spend the money?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If you do not stop me we will go ahead.

The estimates this year are pretty skimpy so far as public works projects in the province of Nova Scotia are concerned. I took a look at the Sydney end. There is $100,000 for a new public building in Sydney, and provision for a breakwater at Glace Bay. There does not seem to be anything else in the whole area, and you have a bad unemployment problem there. I still want to find out if you can explain what you are going to do with the $4 million that you owe us.
They are going to build the Canso bridge.
There is a special appropriation for that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My hon. friend understands that on the 31st of March every year unexpended money reverts to the consolidated revenue fund. We have to vote new estimates every year because they lapse on the 31st of March. When such amounts lapse they are taken care of by revotes, and you can see them all through the estimates. We do not drop a project. We keep on working, and when the plans are ready and the season is proper we proceed with those works. The money will be spent.
The minister spoke of his good intentions. I have heard that the road to Hull is paved with good intentions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: As to the vote for public buildings in Nova Scotia, I note from the details on page 222 that there is $86,000 included for a public building at Barrington Passage of which $25,000 is a revote. If my memory serves me correctly, we voted the $25,000 on the 10th of December last year. I should like to ask the minister two questions. Was anything done after December 10, 1949, with respect to proceeding with the public building at Barrington Passage? I should also like to know what else is covered by the $86,000 in addition to whatever was covered by the $25,000 voted last December.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Remember that last year's main estimates were prepared in November, 1948. Then we had a session in the spring of 1949.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And an election.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
We got three-quarters of the estimates through. Then we had an election and lost a good many friends. When we came back in the fall we had another session, and all we did was to vote the amounts that had been prepared in the fall of 1948.
Supply-Public Works

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The $25,000 was a supplementary estimate.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Then my argument is still stronger. From that time up to the 31st of March we thought we would acquire a site and retain architects to prepare plans. We started off in headquarters and estimates were prepared as to what it was thought could be spent on that building during the fiscal year 1950-51. I am told now that the estimated cost of the building, to be spent in 1950-51, is $86,000. That is why we ask for this vote.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What does it include?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is the estimate of the total cost of the building.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What was the $25,000 for? Was that just to acquire a site? Surely not.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That was the amount we thought we would spend during the last fiscal year, and it was not spent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is it not possible to break down the $86,000 into what the original $25,000 was for and what the additional $61,000 is for?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I cannot do that now because I do not know the price we will pay for the site. I do not know the exact amount we will have to pay to the architects. We have not asked for tenders yet, and I do not know the amount of the contract. In preparing the estimates I take the advice of the architects in my department. They say they need a building containing so much space. It will be fireproof, it will be on a site of these dimensions, and it will be this and that. They say that should reasonably cost around $86,000. When my estimates come up next year I will give you all the details because the project will be advanced.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I should like to call the minister's attention to some answers he gave a short time ago in response to questions. I placed upon the order paper having to do with the erection of a public building at Woodstock, New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Did you ask those questions for the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Well, he is not here at the moment, so I cannot get the information from him. At any rate, as appears at page 3466 and 3467 of Hansard for June 12, 1950, I asked the minister:
1.	Did Mr. T. S. Hunter, district architect of the Department of Public Works, recently (between May 1 and May 18, 1950) visit Woodstock, New Brunswick, for the purpose of investigating possible sites for a new post office building in the town of Woodstock?
2.	Did Mr. Hunter confer with Mr. D. R. Bishop?
3.	If so, did such conference relate to the possible site for a new post office building in Woodstock?
The answers to those first three questions were yes. So far so good. Question No. 4 was:
4.	Who is Mr. D. R. Bishop and what official position, if any, does he hold in relation to federal government matters?
There are several more questions-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What was the answer?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The answer to questions 4, 5, 6 and 7 was "Not known".

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is true. I do not know this Bishop; I do not know who he is.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Let me carry on and I may tell you.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, you know? Then you do not need information from me; you are giving me information.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Well, if I give the minister some information he may be able to go on from there and answer some further questions. In reply to the question as to who this Mr. Bishop is, the minister says that is not known. He knows Mr. T. S. Hunter conferred with him, but he does not know who Mr. Bishop is.
My next question was:
5.	Has Mr. D. R. Bishop been a candidate in any federal election campaign for the electoral district of Victoria-Carleton? If so, for what party?

Again the answer is "Not known." I should have thought the Minister of Public Works would be a better party man than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not know all our supporters.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
He will find from the records that Mr. D. R. Bishop was the Liberal candidate in Victoria-Carleton last June and polled a certain number of votes, but lost the election. Now we have the answer to that question; Mr. D. R. Bishop is the defeated Liberal candidate in Victoria-Carleton. That is the man with whom Mr. T. S. Hunter conferred with regard to a site for this post office, a man whom the Minister of Public Works does not know.
Next question:
6.	Does he have anything to do with federal government patronage in or for the electoral district of Victoria-Carleton?
Again the answer is "Not known." The minister did not say "No"; he just said "Not known."

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have never seen the man; he has never spoken to me, and I do not recall ever having received a letter from him. What would you want me to answer?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The next question was:
7.	If so, is the patronage he handles restricted to matters relating to the Post Office Department and the selecting of sites for post office and customs buildings, etc., or does he handle patronage for other federal government departments, and if so what departments?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am a bad witness; I don't know.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Yes, that is the answer; the minister does not know. Well, the inference from the answer to that question is that it could be that Mr. D. R. Bishop is handling the patronage for the federal government down in Victoria-Carleton.
Where is the patronage you are talking about? You are suggesting there is some.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Certainly it is not denied by the minister in replying to that question.

Ask him the
question.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
If the hon. member for Ottawa East wants the information, I have it here. If the minister and the hon. member would like to know I can tell them that this Mr. D. R. Bishop not long ago published a paid advertisement in the Hartland Observer, a paper published down in the constituency of Victoria-Carleton, pointing out that he had documents to prove that he. not the sitting

member, was the person responsible lor contracts, the choosing of sites and various other things that are being done by the federal government in Victoria-Carleton.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Could I stop him from doing that?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: My point is that I am amazed to discover that a defeated Liberal candidate seems to have the say which this Mr. D. R. Bishop claims to have with respect to various matters in that constituency. I hear members on this side of the house say they know who handles the patronage in their own constituencies, particularly some of the members coming from eastern Canada. I do not know who handles it in Winnipeg North Centre, nor do I want to know, though it may be some hon. members on the Liberal side will know. I am complaining as strongly as I can against this whole business of patronage. We had it here the other day, when the hon. member for Temiscouata wanted all the Tories, C.C.F.'ers and Social Crediters fired from the Canadian Commercial Corporation.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: There it is, Mr. Chairman; those Liberals seem to want to run everything on a party basis.
What happened in Saskatchewan when the C.C.F. government got in?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Please; we are on the estimates of the Department of Public Works.
What did Douglas say?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. It seems to me we are discussing item No. 295, which refers to expenditures for the province of New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That's right. Item 295 provides $2,200,000 for public buildings in the province of New Brunswick. If we turn to page 223 we find included in that amount $100,000 for a public building at Woodstock, New Brunswick, and I am talking about that public building.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member was not talking about that public building when I called him to order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Well, I was not too far away from it.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I do not think the hon. member should continue to use expressions such as "I was amazed that defeated Liberal candidates should have the patronage in these ridings". We all know they have; it is not amazing to anyone. Let the hon. member be accurate.
Supply-Public Works

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext:
After all, I have asked a
number of questions in this house concerning patronage. Hon. members know that. Those questions may have been a bit embarrassing at times. It is not surprising to me that some hon. members in various parts of the house, whenever they have these items that confirm that there is patronage, have drawn them to my attention. The member for Victoria-Carleton also gave me a copy of the Sentinel Press from Woodstock, New Brunswick, dated Thursday, May 18, 1950. It was in this copy of the Sentinel Press that there appeared the story of the visit to Woodstock by Mr. T. S. Hunter. The article contained this sentence:
While in Woodstock Mr. Hunter conferred with Mr. D. R. Bishop . . .

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: And others.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Oh, no. The article does
not say "and others". I presume he did, but so far as the Sentinel Press is concerned Mr. Hunter conferred only with Mr. D. R. Bishop. I suggest that this business of patronage is difficult to uproot by a single speech, or even by a dozen questions during the course of the session. But I did hope to draw it to public notice in this way, and that by having it drawn to public attention so well as it was done yesterday by the member for Temiscouata we may see the last of it. I like the Minister of Public Works, and I hate to find signs of it in his department. He is the last minister in the government I would expect to condone it in any way at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am still a live politician, just the same.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I still like the minister. I
hope the minister will be careful when he gets his advice, not only in the constituency of Victoria-Carleton but in all other constituencies, to get it from other than defeated Liberal candidates or even sitting Liberal members. He should get advice from experts in the field.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I cannot let this pass without a few sentences in

reply. When this item was put in my estimates, it was upon the representations of people in whom I have confidence. We looked into the request, and got reports that the need was there. I believe the actual building in Woodstock was erected in 1883. I did not look at the riding in which it was located.
As I explained earlier this afternoon, the first thing we do is to look for a site. We send the resident architect, who happens to be Mr. Hunter, to look over the situation. I am told he saw six or seven people. The report is that amongst the people he saw was one Mr. Bishop. I did not even know that he was the defeated candidate, but that is not against him. Perhaps he knows the place well. You say that he handles the patronage, and he brags about it. That is not within my knowledge. I speak to every member of parliament, defeated candidates, and everyone, and you cannot imagine what advice they give me. I do not always rely on that. I get the officials to go to the place and make a report on the site. If that official goes into Mr. So-and-So's home, I hope you do not blame me for that.

Mr. Chairman, I trust the applause is an indication of approval. With reference to this item, and the details which appear on page 225 which indicate an office building for Hamilton, and the appropriation listed in the amount of $300,000, does it refer to the proposed building at the corner of Caroline and Main streets in Hamilton?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
This amount is required towards the erection of an office building in Hamilton, Ontario, to provide accommodation for the following departments: veterans affairs, unemployment insurance commission, trade and commerce, national defence, labour, transport, agriculture, national revenue, health and welfare, customs and immigration. Strong representations have been made by the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the Minister of Labour regarding the necessity for immediate action.
Plans and specifications have not yet been prepared. However, preparation of them is being undertaken by Mr. Hugh D. Robertson, architect, of Hamilton, Ontario. The tentative estimated cost is $1,250,000. The expenditure for 1949-50 was $116,051.63. A new vote will be requested for 1950-51 of $165,000. The total vote requested for 195051 is $300,000. The hon. member will understand that this is the amount we expect to spend during that year.
The site to be acquired for the proposed building is the Caroline street school property being the block-end bounded by George, Caroline and Main streets. The property has a frontage of 194 feet 5 inches on Caroline street, and depths of 241 feet 3 inches and 235 feet 11 inches on George and Main streets respectively. The property is owned by the Hamilton board of education. Notice of expropriation was filed on this property March 4, 1948. The Hamilton board of education originally forwarded an asking price in the amount of $234,415. However, as a result of negotiations, this offer has been reduced to $215,000, and the department proposes to acquire the property at that reduced figure.
An order in council dated February 24, 1949, authorized an advance payment of $99,000 to the Hamilton board of education from 1948-49 funds. An order in council dated May 17, 1949, authorized the payment of the sum of $215,000 to the Hamilton board of education in full and final settlement of the above-mentioned property at Hamilton, Ontario, such amount to include the advance payment of $99,000.
I noticed the $99,000 payment in last year's estimates. This $300,000 then will not do more than pay the purchase price of the property.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: And pay for the plans and specifications.

Can the minister tell me at what stage the negotiations are at the present time, and how soon work might commence on this project? I know that is a difficult question to answer, because one never

knows how long it is going to take to draw plans. As a matter of fact, this property has been standing idle for some time. I believe negotiations were started about two years ago. Just prior to the election of 1949 the old building was demolished and the land was levelled. In the meantime a few signboards have been erected on the property, and the rumour is abroad that the property is to be resold. I take it the minister's remarks would effectively deny that rumour. I am glad, because the building is vitally needed in Hamilton where the government departments, some of which the minister has mentioned, are housed in various buildings in different sections of the city. When given up by the government departments, the space in these buildings could easily be rented.
At one stage in the proceedings a member made the remark to the Hamilton city council that it was hoped the erection of this building would be commenced this year, so that when the autumn of the year came along and construction trades were in need of work this particular project might ease the local situation. From the minister's remarks I would think that is a rather remote hope. Does the minister expect the work to commence this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have given the list of departments requesting space in that building. We are getting the architect to allot space for veterans affairs and these departments, and he will then draw the plans and specifications according to those requests. I am told that the plans themselves, when these requests are looked after, will take at least six months to prepare. For a building of $1,500,000, my experience has generally been that the plans and specifications take a year to prepare. Then time has to be allowed for the calling of tenders, because the moment we receive those plans we advertise for tenders. The amount we have today in this estimate is the amount we think we will spend during the current fiscal year.
In that event, there could be no hope at all of proceeding this year at least.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would not want to say that. I have been greatly disappointed myself many times by delays in the preparations of plans and specifications. Remember my good friend the hon. member for Queens. He has been waiting a long time but he is not despairing yet.

I may say I am pleased that the architect is in Hamilton. Maybe I can do something from that end.
Supply-Public Works

I should like to quote the example of the hon. member for Hamilton West to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. The hon. member for Hamilton West has been practical in supporting a justified expenditure for her constituency. If the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton had been here,
I wonder if he would have spoken as did the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He probably did so because he did not represent the constituency. As an old politician, I will tell him never to oppose the construction of any public building in any province in Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is that how you got your railroad?

I should like to inquire from the minister if the continuity of plans is going to be followed with respect to the public buildings in Ottawa and in central Canada, having regard to their design and the building materials to be used. I notice a large number of appropriations, including one in Hamilton for a substantial public building. The most important public buildings in Ottawa, including the parliament buildings, are trimmed with stone from Wallace, Nova Scotia. This building, including the peace tower, has Wallace sandstone which is recognized as the equal of the best in the world, if not the best. The fact that it is being used in buildings such as this, in the national museum building, in the Confederation building, in the customs building, in the national research and a number of other buildings in the city shows that it has been recognized as being of the highest quality. Few materials the product of the maritime provinces come to central Canada. I should like to ask the minister what public buildings are under construction at this time, or are being designed, that call for the use of Wallace sandstone.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I understand that in the specifications we cannot say that it has-to be Wallace sandstone. We probably have the word "sandstone" if it is to be that kind of stone.
I think it is usually specified as Wallace sandstone.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am told that we do not do that. That would cut out competition if we just put in this particular stone.
I think that the contractor is required to know what kind of stone is going to be used.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes. He bids on sandstone, and he generally specifies the-quarry from which that stone will come.

Supply-Public Works

I understand that the architects specify the quarry from which the sandstone is to be procured. There is some extremely inferior sandstone, and some inferior sandstone has been used in this building. It came from the United States, and is Ohio sandstone. It was used at the rear of the building and is now sanding off quite badly, but it was recovered from the old parliament buildings which were destroyed by fire. I presume the Department of Public Works of that day thought that they were saving some money by using stone that had already been utilized in the original parliament buildings.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We do specify sandstone of such and such a quality. But we cannot say that it has to come from one quarry or the other quarry. I think that would not be according to the act and that it would not be fair. We have got to give to the owner of every quarry a chance to try to sell his wares. If the quality is there and the price is the lowest, he generally gets the contract.

May I ask the
minister if the stone that is specified will be specified as Canadian sandstone, or as sandstone from Nova Scotia or from the maritime provinces rather than imported sandstone?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is mentioned in the contract, I think. It is Canadian stone. That is what I am told.

I notice that in this item there is an appropriation of $10 million for Ontario. In going down through the various items I find that for the city of Ottawa the items listed here come to $5 million, which is half the appropriation. That may be perfectly in order, but Ontario is quite a sizeable place; and if that amount of money is going to be spent in Ottawa, then of course there is not going to be much left for any other one particular place. I should like to ask about .the item of $200,000 for the east block; it was $400,000 last year and it is $200,000 this year. Does the minister know whether that is going to be all that is required to complete that work?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No. I am sure that it will not be all but at the moment I cannot give you any further information. I mentioned this morning that this is done on a fixed fee contract because we could not get specifications prepared or get anybody to give a firm price on the alterations to be made. We had to go step by step before we found out exactly what should have been done. When we started off on it we were told, after some inspection, that the roof would last a few more years. While we were doing the other

work, we found out that we had to replace that roof immediately. That is what we found in a building that we put up some eighty years ago. I cannot see any other way of proceeding if we want to keep that building. You could argue perhaps that it should have disappeared; but if we had had it torn down, you would have found much objection on the score of interfering with the symmetry of the grounds. These are things that even my department do not like. They are just tricky jobs where you hardly know what they are going to cost. Even contractors do not like them. They will not bid.
I am not complaining about it because I realize that it is long past the time when it should have been taken care of.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: During the war they would not give me any estimate for repairs to buildings.
That is quite true. However, I have another question I should like to ask the minister and that is in regard to the sound reinforcement system for the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I spoke of that this morning.
If it was dealt with then, I shall not pursue the matter.

There is one question the minister did not answer. What departmental buildings are now being projected or are under construction in Ottawa following out the general architectural design of the major buildings now here?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We are putting up the veterans affairs building. The contract for the east part of the veterans building was awarded some five or six weeks ago. Then there is the statistics building on Tunney's pasture. The contract was awarded some time ago. We propose to put up a fireproof building for the 1951 census, which afterwards will become a storage building. It will be on Tunney's pasture. It is a building which we urgently need to take the records from office space buildings which are occupied now, and they have no more space for them. We are also putting up vaults for the film board, because they have become so dangerous that we dare not keep them unless they are put in a fireproof building.
They are so subversive, are they?

In these major departmental buildings is the general architectural design being followed? What are the contract prices for these buildings that have already been let to which the minister has referred?

lowest tenderer?

What is the contract price, there?

He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of my introducing Bill No. 132, an act to amend the Pipe Lines Act passed in 1949, was to insert in section 12 of chapter 20 of the statutes of 1949 in the fourth line of the section the following words:
Whereof the main line shall be located entirely within Canada.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that in 1949 a charter was granted to the Westcoast Transmission Company, and at that time information was given to the house that the intention of the company was to build a line from the Alberta oil fields to the western coast of British Columbia, and from there down the west coast to Bellingham, Everett, Seattle and Portland.	Shortly after the
charter was granted to the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited they made application for another route, namely, down through the Crowsnest pass into the United States, and proposed to build a feeder line back to Vancouver and into the smelter plant at Trail.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, a speech made by myself in the house on April 3, 1950. As recorded at page 1481 of Hansard I said at that time:
All that parliament is being asked to do is to give these companies now applying for a charter the same opportunity and the same privilege as was given to the Westcoast Transmission Company.
That was the purpose of my introducing this bill.
We on this side of the house do not believe in monopolies and. therefore, would like to see some competition. In view of the facts that I have stated will anyone suggest that the Sunray Oil Corporation of Tulsa and Los Angeles or the Pacific Western Oil Corporation of Los Angeles or the Tidewater Associated Oil Company of San Francisco are interested in developing Canada first? The answer is. "Certainly not." If the Westcoast Transmission Company are sincere they will make application immediately to withdraw their application to build outside Canada and state clearly that they will follow an all-Canadian route.

Pipe Lines Act
I understand that shortly after I made that speech in the House of Commons on April 3 the Westcoast Transmission Company showed their sincerity, for which I thank them very much, and made an application to withdraw the proposed construction of a pipe line along the route I formerly mentioned. As you will recall, on April 3 I introduced a bill to amend the act granting a charter to the Westcoast Transmission Company in order that they should be compelled to follow an all-Canadian route. Since that time I have withdrawn that bill because of the fact that the company has now demonstrated its willingness to follow an all-Canadian route.
Since the applications for charters of Prairie Transmission Lines Limited and the Alberta Natural Gas Company were granted by parliament after a long debate in the house and in the committee stage, much information has been obtained which we did not possess before. I am not alarmed at the present time that there will be built outside Canada any pipe line that can reasonably be constructed within Canada itself following an all-Canadian route to the west coast. I have great faith in our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), the leader of the Liberal party. I should like to refer to a statement which he made on May 5, as recorded at page 2229 of Hansard:
I am not going to suggest that the protracted debates in this parliament about the desirability of an all-Canadian pipe line for the gas and oil of Alberta has been a waste of time. It has aroused public opinion as to the desirability of doing that if it is possible. I would expect that that would not be lost from the point of view of the members of the board of transport commissioners and that they would not lightly disregard the unanimous desires of Canadians that their own territory be used to the' greatest possible advantage. I would expect that when they got an application and before they approved anything, they would want to be shown that there is or there is not a practicable way of doing it without going out of Canada. I would expect that they will require the applicants to satisfy them that surveys of the various routes mentioned in this discussion have been made.
I do not claim to know enough about the topographical conditions, about the mountain passes, to be able to formulate an opinion as to whether or not they present insuperable difficulties. But if I were a member of the board charged by parliament with the responsibility of making that kind of a decision and were called upon to exercise my judgment, I would want pretty full evidence that it could not be done in Canada before I would put my signature to a plan or project that was not going to be carried out in Canada.
As has been pointed out by many members of the house, owing to the fact that these other applications are before the board of transport commissioners, I cannot see any reason why the board would grant a charter outside Canada if it were possible to build the line within Canada. I am not one of
IMr. Sinnott.l
those who believe in boards or commissions.
I think the more power that is left within parliament itself the better the interests of the people of Canada, or of any other country, will be safeguarded.
In view of the fact that there are enough companies now granted charters to compete in building these pipe lines, and having the assurance of the Prime Minister that the line itself will be constructed in Canada if at all possible, I am led to believe that at the present time I should drop this amendment and leave it to the board of transport commissioners to carry out the views expressed in the remarks of the Prime Minister which I have just quoted. I therefore ask, Mr. Speaker, to have permission to drop the bill at this time, and if necessary introduce it again at a later date.

Perhaps I should begin by saying that while I listened to most of the other debates, in many respects this I believe is the most unique to which I have listened for a long time. Part of that uniqueness arises from a situation which, I suggest, does no credit to the House of Commons, and particularly to some members of it. I refer to the denial of the privilege being extended to an hon. member to withdraw a motion he had proposed.
Whether this has been done facetiously, or with a deliberate intent to embarrass the hon. member, or for whatever reason it may have been, it is, sir, a discourtesy which has been unusual in my experience here; and I should not like to let it pass without drawing attention to it.
Further than that, as a member of the House of Commons I resent the suggestion that if a member desires to withdraw a motion, or anything he has said or done in the house, having changed his mind, he has done something discreditable-because that was the implication which was made deliberately, apparently. There are not many who have sat in the House of Commons longer than I have, and I say that if we were to banish from the membership of the house not only those who have changed their minds, but some who have boxed the compass on almost every question that has come up, we would be a badly discredited lot. There were at least two members in the last parliament who, if they never spoiled their ballot, certainly did everything with it that a man could do-and I suppose we have some runners-up for that record.
As a member from Manitoba I resent the suggestion that there is anything discreditable in a member wishing to withdraw his motion. As I heard him giving his reasons for changing his mind, it seemed to me that they were more reasonable and cogent than any of the reasons I have heard thus far for refusing the withdrawal of his motion.
The whole question of pipe lines legislation has been debated in the House of Commons during two sessions of parliament. The house has given its decision on four separate occasions this year, and it seems to me that any attempt to revive a discussion of matters which were settled by the house on those four occasions smacks either of facetiousness or of insincerity.

The hon. member who introduced the bill, realizing that the house had made its decision this session, was prepared to let the matter drop and, in those circumstances, it seems to me a bit unusual-and perhaps not; hon. members may use this occasion to get in a parting shot on the subject-to attempt to make it appear as though there was something unreasonable, improper or insincere in his attitude. Obviously many other communities in Canada are just as great fire hazards as were Rimouski and Cabano, and I suggest that some consideration should be given to the drafting of a municipal fire code so that in communities so vulnerable as were these two in Quebec, proper precautions may be taken to prevent similar occurrences. I realize that this may be a little beyond anything now being done by the department. I also appreciate the splendid work being done by the underwriters' association in this connection. But, Mr. Chairman, I am afraid there will be other great fires in Canada unless steps are taken to prevent them.
Here we have the engineering branch of a federal department, and insurance is a federal matter. When we have a holocaust such as we had at Rimouski it becomes a federal responsibility to furnish relief. I am merely suggesting that an ounce of prevention be applied by the department in drawing up a code. Many communities built in the last half century are fire hazards of the worst type, and it was only due to merciful Providence that the loss of life in those two great fires was not very large. I believe the federal authority should at least consider the possibility of drawing up some statutory regulations which over a period of
Supply-Public Works
years would eradicate these fire hazards. I know it cannot be done all at once. I know this may be something new, and perhaps outside the jurisdiction of this department; but we know that when we have a great fire the federal authorities have to provide relief, and rightly so. This is how they
explain it. Suppose I have $400,000. Hon. members know how we proceed; we must have authority from the comptroller of the treasury to encumber these estimates as we give out contracts. When the amount of $400,000 has been completely encumbered the comptroller of the treasury will not grant us another nickel even to undertake pressing or urgent works. Under the Consolidated Kevenue and Audit Act he is not empowered to do so. He will place a limit on the department, and we will not be able to have pressing work done which may be required by a storm or any other unforeseen event. This commitment power, however, gives us the authority to go ahead and give out a contract without paying for it during this fiscal year, voting the estimate next year. The officials of finance, treasury board and comptroller of the treasury developed this method so the government would not be left without authority if something unforeseen should happen.

Once we decide to build the float we were discussing a moment ago I bring in a vote to cover it and the house gives me authority to proceed. These maintenance and repair items, however, arise as time goes on. Our offices report that this building needs paint, or that building must be repartitioned, or something must be done somewhere else to keep the building in good condition. Under these votes we are not authorizing the department to go out and let contracts; we are giving the department authority to keep these buildings in a good state of repair. That is the difference. If we were to say this $400,000 should go for a building in St. John's we would go ahead and buy the site, prepare the plans, ask for tenders, and give the contract, because parliament would have authorized the construction of that building. The amount we would put in

I should like to say just a few words on this item. Last January one of my constituents, Allen Ronaghan, wrote me a letter which reads as follows:
I am enclosing a picture which I have cut from the Edmonton Journal. I feel that it speaks loudly enough itself without too many comments from me!
I wish that I could say I was as proud of the national gallery building as I am of the services that it renders to all Canada.
Whenever you get a chance in the house tell them that there are some "out west" who would like to see more money spent on the national gallery. Perhaps it'll humour them into taking some action!
I am.
Yours truly,
Allen Ronaghan
He sent along the picture which he had taken from the Edmonton Journal, and which I am going to send over to the minister in a moment. It is headed: "National gallery forced into corridor". Below the picture we have these words:
Officials of the national gallery of Canada say their work is hampered seriously by an acute shortage of space in the gallery building-one wing of the national museum at Ottawa, H. O. McCurry left, gallery director, and Dr. R. H. Hubbard, curator of Canadian art, kneel in a crowded corridor to examine a still-life by Canadian artist Goodridge Roberts.
He added a footnote as follows:
This picture published in other countries would be marvellous advertising for us, wouldn't it?
I do not feel that hon members, or the minister in particular, want to have pictures of this kind circulated. With Mr. Ronaghan I would like to add my word that something be done. I am of course aware that we have had a commission sitting dealing with art, literature and so forth, and they may possibly have a recommendation to make in connection with this national gallery building. I am sending this picture over to the minister for his examination.
